register_revisions.note: Eight essays had no register entry at all, so the owed count tracked only pre-declared debts and could not fall when an unregistered essay landed. Twelve records were added for essays 03, 05, 09, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 17. The owed number stopped being a partial tally and became the whole remaining required work -- which is why it rose while five essays were shipping.

The depends_on state was added, so a proof conditional on an assumption made elsewhere is no longer filed as a second assumption. The assumption count therefore changed meaning: it now counts ROOT imports, not every record resting on one. A better metric, and a different one.

Essay 13 derived the dimension formula instead of quoting it, which closed three owed items -- the formula itself, essay 25's level-2 computation, and the pre-registered valence-formula plan. The assumption count went UP, from 20 to 21, and that is the honest direction: 13-valence-formula was retired and replaced by the two imports the Riemann-Hurwitz derivation actually spends. Discharging an assumption by deriving it can cost more root imports than it saves, and the register is supposed to show that rather than hide it.

proof_register.text: A counterexample at any exponent $n\geq3$ would give one at exponent $4$ or at an odd prime exponent.
$x^4+y^4=z^2$ has no solution in positive integers, and therefore Fermat's Last Theorem holds for $n=4$.
Kummer's regular-prime criterion and his theorem for regular prime exponents are stated.
The first case of Fermat's Last Theorem for $n=3$ is ruled out in the Eisenstein integers.
The second case for $n=3$ is outlined, not proved; the unit analysis inside the descent remains compressed.
Unique factorisation is shown to fail by an explicit double factorisation in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$.

Restriction to finite Galois subextensions is compatible and determines an element, so $G_{\mathbb{Q}}\cong\varprojlim\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ is profinite. Continuity into a non-discrete target such as $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_\ell)$ means every layer $G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n)$ is determined at a finite level -- not that $\rho$ factors through a finite quotient, which for a non-CM curve it does not.

$\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q})\cong(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$ via $\sigma_a(\zeta)=\zeta^a$, and $\mathrm{Frob}_\ell=\sigma_\ell$, so the cyclotomic character satisfies $\chi(\mathrm{Frob}_\ell)=\ell$ -- the computation essay 10 assumed when it wrote $\det\bar\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_\ell)\equiv\ell$.

The irreducible factors of $\Phi_n$ modulo $\ell$ all have degree equal to the multiplicative order of $\ell$ modulo $n$, so Frobenius predicts how $\ell$ splits; and $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt5)$ is the unique intermediate field of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)$.

proof_register.short: Frobenius elements at unramified primes, as a conjugacy class
proof_register.text: The Frobenius package: $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ acts transitively on the primes above an unramified $\ell$, the decomposition group maps isomorphically onto the residue-field Galois group, and that group is generated by $x\mapsto x^\ell$. Different choices give conjugates, so $\mathrm{Frob}_\ell$ is a conjugacy class.
Irreducibility of the cyclotomic polynomial, giving $[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(n)$ and ensuring every $\sigma_a$ occurs.

proof_register.short: The Galois correspondence, and the existence of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$
proof_register.text: The Galois correspondence between subgroups and intermediate fields for a finite Galois extension, and the existence of the algebraic closure.
$\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ exists as the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ for $|\cdot|_\ell$, is a field, and contains $\mathbb{Q}$ as a dense subfield.
Essay 01's step that coprime factors of a perfect power are themselves powers is proved once, for every exponent, as a statement about valuations.

On the congruence side: every compatible sequence has exactly one digit expansion and every digit string occurs, proved for $\varprojlim\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\mathbb{Z}$ directly, without appeal to completeness or to the identification of the two constructions.
Free modules over $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$ have well-defined rank, and a matrix lies in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_\ell)$ exactly when its determinant has valuation $0$.
The metric and congruence constructions agree: $\mathbb{Z}_\ell\cong\varprojlim\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\mathbb{Z}$.
On the valuation-ring side: $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$ is a ring whose units are the elements of valuation $0$, so it has the single maximal ideal $\ell\mathbb{Z}_\ell$.
The valuation $v_\ell$ is additive on products and ultrametric on sums, with equality when the valuations differ, and $|\cdot|_\ell$ is multiplicative and non-archimedean.

Continuous $\rho:G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to\mathrm{GL}_2(K)$ is defined, in the layer-wise form required by a non-discrete target; reducible means a Galois-stable line, hence two characters and a corner, and semisimple means the corner vanishes.

proof_register.short: Traces of Frobenius determine a semisimple representation
proof_register.text: A semisimple two-dimensional representation is determined up to isomorphism by the traces of Frobenius at almost all primes. This is what makes "these two representations agree" a checkable claim in essays 18 and 25.

Inertia subgroups $I_\ell\subseteq D_\ell\subseteq G_{\mathbb{Q}}$ with $D_\ell/I_\ell$ generated by $\mathrm{Frob}_\ell$; and the conductor $N(\rho)=\prod\ell^{n_\ell}$, with $n_\ell=0$ exactly when $\rho$ is unramified at $\ell$ and $n_\ell=\dim V-\dim V^{I_\ell}$ when the ramification is tame. The general formula in the higher ramification groups is not developed.

Over $\mathbb{F}_\ell$ the diagonalisable matrices with a given characteristic polynomial form a single conjugacy class, verified exhaustively; and the identity and the Jordan block share a characteristic polynomial without being conjugate, so the semisimplicity hypothesis of the trace theorem cannot be dropped.

The quadratic character of $(\mathbb{Z}/5)^\times$ has kernel $\{1,4\}$, the subgroup essay 03 showed fixes $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt5)$, so it is that field as a representation, of conductor $5$; and $\mathbf{1}\oplus\bar\chi$ has trace $1+\ell$, which identifies the conductor-$11$ curve's mod $5$ semisimplification.
For $y^2+y=x^3-x^2$, direct calculation gives $\Delta=-11$ and a short integral model whose discriminant is $6^{12}(-11)$.
The genus-one characterization and existence of a general Weierstrass model are stated; its point at infinity and discriminant are defined; the discriminant criterion for smoothness is stated.
proof_register.short: A genus-one curve has a Weierstrass model, and $\Delta\neq0$ is smoothness

proof_register.text: Associativity of chord-and-tangent addition, and hence the full abelian-group theorem for $E(\mathbb{Q})$, is stated rather than proved.
proof_register.short: Associativity of the chord-and-tangent group law

proof_register.text: The chord-and-tangent rule, rational closure and the short-Weierstrass addition formulas are derived.
The point $(0,0)$ on $y^2+y=x^3-x^2$ is shown by direct calculation to have order $5$.
Complex uniformization $E(\mathbb{C})\cong\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is stated, not proved.
Bad reduction at $\ell$ holds exactly when $\ell$ divides $\Delta_{\min}$, so there are finitely many bad primes and one valuation computation finds them all.
At an additive prime $f_\ell\geq2$, with equality for $\ell>3$, and the primes $2$ and $3$ permit larger exponents.
At a prime of multiplicative reduction the conductor exponent is $f_\ell=1$. This is the only conductor exponent the Fermat argument uses, because the Frey curve is semistable.
proof_register.short: Conductor exponent $f_\ell=1$ at a multiplicative prime

proof_register.text: The Hasse bound $|a_\ell|\leq2\sqrt{\ell}$.
Every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ has a global minimal model. The FLT chain does not need this in general: essay 23 exhibits the Frey curve's minimal model and must prove that model minimal.
The trichotomy good / multiplicative / additive follows from the tangent directions at the unique singular point of the reduced cubic, and $a_\ell\in\{0,\pm1\}$ at a bad prime names the type.
Given the conductor exponents, $N_E$ is square-free exactly when $E$ is semistable, and a semistable curve has $N_E=\operatorname{rad}(\Delta_{\min})$.
Reduction at a good prime is injective on torsion of order coprime to $\ell$, which is why $5$ divides every point count of the conductor-$11$ curve.
$y^2+y=x^3-x^2$ is semistable of conductor $11$, split multiplicative at $11$ with $a_{11}=1$; $y^2=x^3+1$ is additive at $2$ and $3$, so it is not semistable.

The Frey curve has full rational $2$-torsion: $x(x-a^p)(x+b^p)$ has three rational roots, so $E[2]\subset E(\mathbb{Q})$, while the conductor-$11$ curve has $E(\mathbb{Q})[2]=\{O\}$. This is the extra structure that may sharpen Mazur's threshold from $p>7$ to $p\geq5$.
For $y^2=x^3+1$: $\psi_3=3x(x^3+4)$, the point $(0,1)$ has order $3$ by a triple tangency, and exactly three of the nine points of $E[3]$ are rational.

$E[n]\cong(\mathbb{Z}/n)^2$ in characteristic zero, proved on the complex torus: $\frac1n\Lambda/\Lambda$ is an $n\times n$ grid because a lattice has two generators. Conditional on essay 07's uniformization, and on nothing else; the $n=2$ and $n=3$ cases are checked independently by the division polynomials.

The $2$-division cubic $4x^3+b_2x^2+2b_4x+b_6$ gives $\#E[2]=4$ with $E[2]\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$; $\psi_3$ gives $\#E[3]=9$; and the Tate module $T_\ell(E)=\varprojlim E[\ell^n]$ is free of rank $2$ over $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$, which is why the representations are $2\times2$.

$G_{\mathbb{Q}}$ acts on each $E[\ell^n]$ by group automorphisms, because the curve and the group law are defined over $\mathbb{Q}$; in a compatible basis this is $\rho_{E,\ell}:G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_\ell)$, with reduction $\bar\rho_{E,\ell}$.

$\det\rho_{E,\ell}$ is the cyclotomic character, from $e_n(Mv,Mw)=e_n(v,w)^{\det M}$ and Galois-equivariance of the pairing. Complex conjugation inverts roots of unity, so $\det\bar\rho(c)=-1$: every $\bar\rho_{E,\ell}$ is odd, discharging that hypothesis of Ribet's theorem.

$\bar\rho_{E,\ell}$ is reducible exactly when $E$ has a rational subgroup of order $\ell$, since a Galois-stable line in $E[\ell]$ is such a subgroup. The Frey curve's full rational $2$-torsion makes $\bar\rho_{E,2}$ trivial.

A rational subgroup of order $m$ forces the stable line to carry the trivial character, hence $a_\ell\equiv\ell+1\pmod m$ at every good prime -- which is essay 08's divisibility, and which fails for both worked curves at the prime where no such subgroup exists.
The Weil pairing: bilinear, alternating, non-degenerate and Galois-equivariant. Its construction uses divisors on the curve and is not given.

At a good prime $\ell\neq p$, $\bar\rho_{E,p}$ is unramified with $\operatorname{tr}\bar\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_\ell)\equiv a_\ell$ and $\det\equiv\ell$ modulo $p$. Stated rather than derived because $\mathrm{Frob}_\ell$ is constructed in essay 03.

Mazur's isogeny theorem in the form the Frey argument needs: $E/\mathbb{Q}$ has no $p$-isogeny if $p>163$, **or** if $p\geq5$ with $\#E(\mathbb{Q})[2]=4$ and squarefree conductor -- the general list being $\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,37,43,67,163\}$ with $19,43,67,163$ requiring CM. And the N\'eron--Ogg--Shafarevich criterion that $\rho_{E,p}$ is unramified at $\ell\neq p$ exactly when $E$ has good reduction there.

$\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ acts on $\mathbb{H}$ with $\operatorname{Im}(\gamma z)=\operatorname{Im}(z)/|cz+d|^2$; the reduction algorithm shows $\mathcal{F}$ is a fundamental domain; $i$ and $ho$ are the elliptic points, of orders $2$ and $3$; and $\Gamma_0(N)$ has index $N\prod_{q\mid N}(1+1/q)$, with $
u_2$, $
u_3$ and $
u_\infty$ defined -- the four inputs essay 13's formula consumes.

The index matches brute-force coset counting in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/N)$ for $N\leq25$; $\nu_2$ and $\nu_3$ equal the numbers of roots of $x^2+1$ and $x^2+x+1$ modulo $N$ for $N<200$, a route independent of the product formulas; and the genus combination is a non-negative integer for every $N<400$, which jointly constrains all four counts.

proof_register.short: $S$ and $T$ generate $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$; $X_0(N)$ is a compact Riemann surface
proof_register.text: That $S:z\mapsto-1/z$ and $T:z\mapsto z+1$ generate $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, verified here only for matrices of small height; and that $X_0(N)=\mathbb{H}^*/\Gamma_0(N)$ is a compact Riemann surface.

Weight-$k$ modularity is consistent because $(cz+d)^k$ satisfies the cocycle identity, and $-I\in\Gamma_0(N)$ forces $k$ even; periodicity under $T$ gives the $q$-expansion, and holomorphy at the cusps is $\nu_\infty$ separate conditions; $M_k(\Gamma_0(N))$ and its subspace of cusp forms $S_k(\Gamma_0(N))$ are defined -- without which "a weight-2 newform of level $N$" has no referent.

$E_4^3-E_6^2=1728\Delta$ verified as exact power series; and $(\eta(z)\eta(11z))^2$ is normalised with $a_1=1$, has multiplicative coefficients, and matches essay 08's hand-counted $a_\ell$ at every prime below forty -- including the bad prime $11$, where essay 08 used a different formula entirely.

proof_register.short: That $\Delta$ and $(\eta(z)\eta(11z))^2$ are modular of the stated weight and level
proof_register.text: That $\Delta$ and $(\eta(z)\eta(11z))^2$ satisfy the transformation law for weights $12$ and $2$ at levels $1$ and $11$. Their $q$-expansions are computed here; the transformation law itself is not verified.

proof_register.short: A genus-$g$ compact Riemann surface has a $g$-dimensional space of holomorphic differentials
proof_register.text: That the space of holomorphic differentials on a compact Riemann surface of genus $g$ has dimension $g$. Combined with the identification of weight-two forms with invariant differentials, which is derived here, this gives $\dim S_2(\Gamma_0(N))=g(X_0(N))$.

proof_register.short: Riemann--Hurwitz, and the ramification structure of $X_0(N)\to X(1)$
proof_register.text: Riemann--Hurwitz for a covering of compact Riemann surfaces, together with the fact that $X_0(N)\to X(1)$ is ramified only above the two elliptic points and the cusp, with indices dividing $2$ above $i$, dividing $3$ above $\rho$, and unconstrained above the cusp. Substituted into by hand here; the consistency of the resulting counts is checked for every $N<400$.

The ramification data at $N=2$ (one point above $i$ with $e=2$, one above $ho$ with $e=3$, two cusps of widths summing to $3$) gives $g=0$, and at $N=11$ (six above $i$, four above $ho$, cusp widths $1$ and $11$) gives $g=1$; the levels below $400$ where the dimension vanishes are exactly $1$--$10$, $12$, $13$, $16$, $18$, $25$; and $
u_\infty$ enters the genus as a ramification count, separately from the vanishing conditions at the cusps, of which exactly one is redundant at weight two by the residue relation -- $\dim M_2-\dim S_2=
u_\infty-1$, against $
u_\infty$ for $k\geq4$. Substituting $k=2$ into the $k>2$ dimension formula returns $g-1$, not $g$, so the weight-two case is genuinely separate and not a vanishing coefficient.

proof_register.short: A simultaneous Hecke eigenbasis exists for $\gcd(n,N)=1$
proof_register.text: The Petersson product is positive definite, and the Hecke operators $T_n$ with $\gcd(n,N)=1$ preserve $S_k(\Gamma_0(N))$, commute and are self-adjoint. The spectral theorem therefore decomposes the space into simultaneous good-Hecke eigenspaces; at general level these eigenspaces need not yet be one-dimensional.

For $\gcd(n,N)=1$, the coefficient formula $a_r(T_nf)=\sum_{d\mid(r,n)}d^{k-1}a_{rn/d^2}$ gives $a_1(T_nf)=a_n(f)$. Thus for a normalised simultaneous eigenform the good Hecke eigenvalues are its Fourier coefficients, which are multiplicative and satisfy the prime-power recurrence.

proof_register.short: Newform theory, and the level of a newform
proof_register.text: Atkin--Lehner--Li theory preserves the old/new decomposition under the full Hecke algebra, turns a good-Hecke eigenvector in the newspace into a unique normalized full-Hecke eigenform, and assigns every eigensystem a unique primitive level. Imported: the bad-prime adjoint and multiplicity-one machinery. Without it "the level" in Ribet's theorem is undefined.

The two degeneracy images $f_{11}(q)$ and $f_{11}(q^2)$ span $S_2(\Gamma_0(22))$, share every good Hecke eigenvalue, and satisfy $[U_2]=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-2&1\\-2&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; hence the whole level-$22$ space is old, the newspace is zero, and $U_2$ is not Hermitian.
Eichler–Shimura will be stated, not proved.

$L(E,s)$ and $L(f,s)$ as Euler products, and the analytic continuation and functional equation. Motivating rather than load-bearing: modularity is stated representation-theoretically, so the chain never evaluates an $L$-function.
The Modularity Theorem will be stated, not proved.
Wiles's deformation-theoretic machinery will be described as an anatomy, not presented as a proof.
Langlands–Tunnell will be stated, not proved.
A normalised hypothetical Fermat solution produces the Frey curve $y^2=x(x-a^p)(x+b^p)$.
The displayed Frey model has discriminant $16(abc)^{2p}$.

The substitution $x=4X$, $y=8Y+4X$ yields an integral model with $a_1=1$ whose discriminant is $\Delta_{\min}=2^{-8}(abc)^{2p}$, and it is minimal at every prime because $c_4=A^2+AB+B^2$ is a unit at each bad prime -- so the FLT chain needs no appeal to the general existence theorem for minimal models.

The Frey curve has multiplicative reduction at every bad prime -- at odd primes because pairwise coprimality forbids a triple root, and at $2$ because $a_1=1$ makes the tangent cone separable -- hence it is semistable with conductor $\operatorname{rad}(abc)$.
$E$ is modular of level $\operatorname{rad}(abc)$, by applying essay 18's Modularity Theorem to the semistability proved in this essay. Conditional on that theorem, and on nothing else.

What each normalisation buys: $A\equiv-1\pmod4$ and $16\mid B$ give integrality of the minimal model, while the extra factor of $2$ in $32\mid B$ is what makes $2$ a bad prime and puts it in the conductor.

$N(\bar\rho_{E,p})=2$. At an odd bad prime $v_\ell(\Delta_{\min})=2p\,v_\ell(abc)$ is a multiple of $p$, so the prime drops out of the conductor; at $2$, $v_2=2p\,v_2(b)-8\equiv-8\not\equiv0$ because $p\nmid8$, so $2$ survives, tamely, with $n_2=1$.

Full rational $E[2]$ forces $4\mid\#\tilde E(\mathbb{F}_\ell)$, and with Hasse this pins $a_3=0$, $a_5=\pm2$, $a_7\in\{0,\pm4\}$, $a_{17}\in\{\pm2,\pm6\}$. Each makes $a_\ell^2-4\ell$ a non-square modulo $p$, proving irreducibility when the witness prime has good reduction -- so $\bar\rho$ is irreducible for $p=5$ unless $21\mid abc$ and for $p=7$ unless $85\mid abc$. Derived here, not sourced; no further uniform witness exists below 400.

proof_register.short: Ramification at a multiplicative prime: unramified iff $p\mid v_\ell(\Delta_{\min})$
proof_register.text: At a prime $\ell\neq p$ of multiplicative reduction, $\bar\rho_{E,p}$ is unramified exactly when $p$ divides $v_\ell(\Delta_{\min})$, and is otherwise tamely ramified with $n_\ell=1$. This is Serre's level recipe in the semistable case, and it is what converts essay 23's valuations into ramification data.
$\bar\rho_{E,p}$ arises from a finite flat group scheme over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ -- a condition at $p$ itself, separate from the primes $\ell\neq p$, and required by Ribet's theorem.

The final contradiction is assembled conditionally on exactly three inputs -- modularity (essay 18), Ribet's theorem, stated here, and finiteness at $p$ (essay 24) -- and the collection's full FLT conclusion additionally on essay 02's outlined second case for $n=3$. Nothing else is external: the irreducibility threshold and the conductor of $\bar\rho$ are settled in essay 24, and the dimension formula, once assumption (F), is derived in essay 13.
The level-$2$ arithmetic is computed, and the formula it evaluates is derived in essay 13 rather than quoted, so the closing computation is no longer conditional on a formula owed elsewhere.
Ribet's level-lowering theorem is stated with the hypotheses used by the closing argument.
